summary:
The Bahamas decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct on 16 May 1991 through the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act. Nothing in the sources indicates that a visitor can be prosecuted for consensual sexual conduct.

Transgender and intersex people hold no statutory protection. Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United launched the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign in April 2016 stating that no laws protect transgender and intersex Bahamians, and its member Torri Culmer has campaigned against the dismissal of trans and intersex workers from their jobs.

The constitutional guarantee against discrimination does not extend to sexual orientation or gender identity. The 2006 Constitutional Reform Commission did not regard sexual orientation as deserving of protection, and proposals to include it in a draft constitution were blocked by members citing religious opposition. A clause banning sexual-orientation discrimination in employment was removed from the 2001 Employment Bill shortly after passage. The Data Protection (Privacy of Personal Information) Act 2003 treats 'sexual life' as sensitive personal data, but no enacted non-discrimination provision covering gender identity appears anywhere in the sources.

There are no national hate-crime laws, and discrimination in healthcare or education on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal. The sources record no HIV-specific and no trans-specific care provisions.

Documents and relationship recognition are restrictive. The Marriage Act defines marriage as between a man and a woman, same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and same-sex households are denied the rights given to opposite-sex married couples. In 2011 former Minister of State Zhivargo Laing stated that a marriage is void if it is between persons of the same sex, describing this as a community standard. The 2016 referendum bills were not inclusive of transgender or intersex people. The criminal code sets the age of consent at 16 for heterosexual acts and 18 for same-sex acts.

An official statement points the other way. In May 1998 National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson announced that the military, prison service and police do not discriminate, and the sources record no prohibition on LGBT citizens serving in those forces.

Official and political hostility is documented. Government member Leslie Miller publicly called for the 'Exile of Transgender out of the Bahamas,' urging financial contributions to relocate transgender people to a private island and pledging $1,000 toward it. Former Prime Minister Perry Christie stated in 2013 that he did not believe in same-sex marriage and said in 2016 that a referendum would not legalise it, defining marriage as between male and female determined at birth.

Violence against LGBT visitors has occurred. On 8 May 2017 Adrian Brown, 24, Jamaica-born and US-resident, was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being targeted and beaten because he is gay at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival, and said he wanted charges laid. A 2009 murder victim, a homosexual HIV-positive man, was killed by a defendant acquitted using a 'gay panic' defence, and nine murders of gay men between 2001 and 2015 remain unsolved.

The social environment constrains visibility. There are no exclusively gay bars or clubs, the Nassau scene is underground, and LGBT groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden. Police raided a gay party in downtown Nassau on 6 October 2007 with no arrests, and the Ministry of Tourism later apologised. Groups of LGBT tourists have been protested, including church-group opposition to a 2004 cruise, a 1998 protest against a lesbian cruise, and the September 2007 formation of an anti-gay committee by the Bahamas Christian Council. In 2016 the Canadian government issued travel advice warning gay couples about the risk of homophobia in the Bahamas.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion is sharply opposed to legal recognition of same-sex relationships: 85.5% strongly disapproved of same-sex marriage in 2015 against 10.6% approving, and over 84% strongly disapproved of a gay or lesbian politician in 2013 with 12% positive.

Many Bahamians belong to conservative Christian denominations treating homosexuality and cross-dressing as decadence, and politicians have been leery of publicly supporting LGBT-rights legislation. Cultural and media controls reflect the same climate: the Plays and Films Control Board banned Brokeback Mountain in March 2006 and attempted to block a public-square screening of Children of God on 24 June 2011, though the government overruled it.

The Communications Act 2009 empowers the national communications regulator to issue codes of practice against content likely to incite hatred or vilify persons on the basis of sexual preference, which is the nearest instrument to a speech-based protection in the sources.

In 2005 an 18-year-old beauty queen had her crown stripped after confirming she was a lesbian. In 2013 and 2016 former Prime Minister Perry Christie ruled out same-sex marriage, and a government member's call to exile transgender people shows that hostility in the sources is directed at transgender people specifically rather than only at gay and lesbian people.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses change of legal gender markers, identity documents or passport gender markers for transgender visitors or residents, so that question is unresolved here rather than answered.

No source addresses entry, visa, border or airport screening procedures that could expose a visitor's transgender status; nothing in the inventory supports a finding either way.

The disposition of the May 2017 assault complaint by Adrian Brown is not sourced; the inventory records the attack, the treatment at Doctors Hospital and his stated wish that charges be laid, but no charging decision or outcome.

Whether the May 1998 non-discrimination statement by Frank Watson reflects current policy is unresolved; the inventory gives no later official statement on the same point.

The inventory does not state whether any charge or penalty has been brought under the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act since decriminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct on 16 May 1991, so enforcement patterns beyond the absence of documented prosecution cannot be confirmed.

No source documents legal frameworks for hate-crime sentencing enhancements, partner visa recognition or conjugal visitation for transgender visitors; these are not sourced and should not be read as absent or present.
